lead: Eyelid exposure describes how much eyelid skin shows between the lash line and the brow or fold when the eyes are open. In looksmaxxing circles, little upper eyelid exposure (UEE) is associated with the "hunter eyes" look, while more exposure is associated with "prey" or tired-looking eyes.

People discuss it because it changes how alert and intense the eye area appears. Published research uses different vocabulary (lid position, margin reflex distance, ptosis, blepharoplasty), and no study has measured "eyelid exposure" as the forums define it.

paras: Members report working with the surrounding features: lower or fuller brow shaping, lash and liner styling, sleep and routine changes, and posture of the gaze (so-called squinting). Some ask about surgical options such as upper blepharoplasty or fat grafting, which are performed by oculofacial surgeons.

Surgery around the eyelids carries standard operative risks such as asymmetry, dry eye and scarring, and is done by licensed surgeons. Lid position can also change with illness, so a sudden change in how much lid shows is a reason clinicians recommend an eye exam.

angle.text: People use the idea to diagnose what makes their eye area look tired or heavy and to choose brow, lash and styling changes, or to ask surgeons about eyelid procedures. The goal is a lid-to-brow relationship that looks more alert.

lead: Eyelid exposure is a looksmaxxing term for how much eyelid skin is visible when the eyes are open and relaxed. Upper eyelid exposure (UEE) is the most discussed form: the band of skin between the lash line and the brow bone or lid crease. Lower eyelid exposure, the sclera (white) or skin showing below the iris, is discussed less often [1][2][3].

The concept sits at the centre of the community distinction between "hunter eyes" and "hooded" or "prey" eyes. Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes hunter eyes as a positive canthal tilt, little to no upper eyelid exposure and low-set eyebrows, giving an eye area likened to that of a predatory animal [4]. Members use the idea to explain why some faces read as intense and alert and others as tired, and to decide which features to work on: brow position, lash and liner styling, habitual eye posture, or consultations about eyelid and brow surgery [1][2][5].

Clinical literature does not use the community term. It describes lid position through measures such as margin reflex distance and through conditions such as ptosis, where the upper lid sits low [6]. Upper eyelid surgery is a long-established field, with techniques aimed at rejuvenating the lid and brow [7], and plastic-surgery practices describe hooded or exposed upper lids in terms of ageing, genetics, excess skin and brow descent [8].

paras: Upper eyelid exposure refers to the visible stretch of upper lid when the eyes are open in a neutral expression. On looksmax.org, users post photos and ask how to limit exposure, noting that it can look more prominent early in the morning or after smoking [1]. Others reply that what the original poster perceives as lid is really brow position, since a low-set brow can hide the lid while a higher brow reveals more of it [2].

Lower eyelid exposure is the mirror concept: how much sclera or lower-lid skin shows beneath the iris. Threads on the topic exist alongside the upper-lid ones, again framed as an eye-area feature that members try to assess from photographs [3]. The upper and lower measures are usually discussed together with canthal tilt as parts of one overall "eye area" read [4].

The upper lid is raised mainly by the levator palpebrae superioris, which retracts the lid to expose the cornea; weakness or paralysis of that muscle produces ptosis. The lids also contain tarsal plates lying beneath the orbital septum, and the shape of the upper lid crease varies between people and populations, with single, low and double creases described among East Asian lids [9].

Ophthalmology describes resting lid position with the marginal reflex distance, the distance from the pupil centre to the edge of the upper lid, and recognises causes of low lid position that are neurogenic, myogenic, aponeurotic with ageing, mechanical, or drug or toxin related [6]. These categories concern medical drooping rather than the aesthetic exposure the forums discuss. Clinical pages on hooded upper lids list ageing skin laxity, inherited features, dermatochalasis (excess upper lid skin), ptosis, myasthenia gravis and Horner's syndrome as contributors [8].

Because the position of the lid can change with health, clinicians describe a sudden or unexplained change in how the lids sit as something to have examined. Thyroid eye disease, for example, is a recognised condition that affects the eye surface and surrounding tissues [10].

According to Wikipedia, looksmaxxing began on incel and manosphere message boards in the 2010s, where the PSL forums (PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net) developed rating scales for faces, and it reached TikTok in the early 2020s, where mostly male creators popularised it as self-improvement [4]. Eye-area vocabulary such as hunter eyes and canthal tilt travelled with it, and eyelid exposure became a standard item in face-analysis threads and rating tools.

Forum threads describe several approaches. Members talk about adjusting eyebrow shape, lash and liner styling, and "squintmaxxing", habitually narrowing the eyes to lower the visible lid; one poster describes tiring of squinting as a coping habit and asks whether it changes anything over time [2]. Threads on eyelid exposure and eyebrows treat brow height and shape as the main variable that can be altered without surgery [5].

Some members ask whether surgery or fat grafting could change exposure. Responses are mixed, and some say that options are limited and that the main workaround is styling [1][2]. Guides and videos in the same community also promote eye-muscle exercises, lid and brow posture, and injectables such as neuromodulators, though these are community claims rather than the subject of published studies on the term.

Upper blepharoplasty and related lid and brow techniques are described in the plastic surgery literature as ways to rejuvenate the upper eyelid and brow, including newer modifications that use less invasive approaches [7]. A plastic surgeon's educational page describes upper blepharoplasty as removing excess skin and fat through an incision in the lid crease, an endoscopic brow lift when brow descent contributes, and non-surgical options such as injections that lift the brow by a millimetre or two for a few months, soft tissue volume restoration and thread lifts. It notes that all surgery carries risks and that swelling and bruising can last up to two weeks after blepharoplasty [8]. These procedures are mostly designed to reduce excess skin or lift the brow, which is the opposite direction from some community goals, since hooded eyes generally have more skin and less visible lid.

Eyelid surgery carries standard operative risks such as asymmetry, dry eye and scarring, and is done by licensed oculofacial or plastic surgeons [7][8]. Lid position can also change with illness; sudden changes are a reason clinicians recommend an eye examination [6][10]. Non-surgical styling approaches such as brow and lash work carry the usual cosmetic cautions.

No studies found. Related published work covers eyelid surgery techniques [7] and lid-position disorders such as ptosis [6], but none measures eyelid exposure as the term is used in looksmaxxing, and none tests whether exposure affects perceived attractiveness or alertness.

lore.intro: Eyelid exposure appears in many looksmax.org threads, often alongside hunter-eyes, canthal tilt and brow discussions [1][2][5].

claims.claim: Minimal upper eyelid exposure gives "hunter eyes".
Squinting can reduce visible eyelid over time.
What looks like eyelid exposure is often really brow position.
Exposure fluctuates with sleep, smoking and time of day.
Fat grafting or surgery can change exposure, but options are limited.
Eye-muscle exercises and lid posture can lower exposure.
